name: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS)
gap: The neighborhood growth pillar (scoring/neighborhood.py) currently draws on development/rezoning activity, transit access, planned catalysts, crime, and Census ACS demographics (census_acs.py), but has no direct local-labor-market signal -- employment growth and unemployment rate are standard leading indicators for housing demand that aren't represented anywhere in the current metric set.
coverage: national (~7,600 areas: counties, cities, metro areas, metro divisions, states)
history_available: BLS LAUS series generally extend back to the 1990s or earlier depending on area, available via bulk time-series files
license: Public domain US government data; bulk flat files and the Series Report tool need no login; the full BLS Public Data API needs a free registration key for higher query limits, but a smaller number of daily queries works unregistered
cost: Free; registered API keys get materially higher daily query limits than unregistered access (specific numbers not independently confirmed against bls.gov/developers this run)
access_method: BLS Public Data API (v2, JSON, optional free key) for series by ID, or bulk downloadable flat files for broader pulls
verification_caveats: Could not reach bls.gov directly this run (sandbox DNS/proxy issue) -- confirm the exact registered vs. unregistered query limits and the current API terms before implementing

No quantitative correlation against FHFA HPI/Zillow ZORI was run (evaluate_series.py doesn't exist yet) -- unemployment/employment-growth as a leading indicator for housing appreciation is a reasonable prior but unverified for this project's specific markets
recommendation_note: A legitimate gap-filler for the neighborhood growth pillar and genuinely national, but it's the weakest of the five candidates here: it's one more general-economy input alongside several the project already has (ACS demographics, development/rezoning activity), rather than fixing a concrete hardcoded assumption or missing pillar the way the other four do. Worth a future look, but lower priority than FHFA HPI, FRED mortgage rates, FEMA NRI, or HUD FMR.
